## Analysis at each round
### Round 1
There are no trials yet. The starting network scored 0.000 on both seeds, but we don't know whether training success was also near 0. Finishing an exact build needs every brick correct. A brick's landing layer is the highest filled cell under its whole footprint, so judging a placement means comparing the build and target columns at every cell the brick covers. The starting head pools learned features with max, min and mean, which may not pass on enough per-cell detail for that. Round 1 splits the test: (a) recipe only on the starting network, with fewer PPO epochs for about 1.85x the samples, longer credit assignment (gamma 0.99, lambda 0.95) and minibatches twice as large, the same as the default 128; (b) a head that joins per-cell column features at each cell of the footprint, with about the same compute (r≈1) and the default recipe; (c) both. While dev success stays at 0, I'll rank by training success.

### Round 2
All three round-1 trials scored 0.0 on dev and 0.0 on training success, as did the starting network. Training success is also 0, so the problem is learning itself, not generalisation. Neither the 2-epoch, gamma 0.99 recipe nor the footprint-concat head made any measurable difference. Nothing here separates their effects from seed noise. Trials take about 67 s, far under the 900 s limit, so time is not a constraint. The step budget is set by FLOPs, and a ratio below 1 counts as 1, so a smaller network gets no extra steps. The biggest lever left is samples: ppo_epochs = 1 gives about 426k steps, roughly 3.3 times the default. This round tests that lever on the starting network. It also tests it on a new network with the same compute, which adds per-cell column features, deeper residual context and a global broadcast so each cell can see the overall build state. The recipe adds slightly sharper entropy (0.005) and gamma 0.98. The third candidate varies the recipe on the new network (higher lr, longer rollouts) to check how robust the result is.

### Round 3
All six trials scored 0 on both dev and training success (last 10%), including runs with 1, 2 and 4 epochs, gamma from 0.95 to 0.99, lr 1e-3 and 2e-3, and three head designs. Because training success is also 0, the problem is learning itself, not generalisation. Neither sample count (131k to 410k steps) nor horizon has made a measurable difference, so I don't think the next gain will come from small recipe tweaks. Time is not a constraint: every run took about 66 s of the 900 s limit. I have untested guesses about the cause. Capacity may be too small for the nonlinear landing-layer comparison. Exploration may collapse, for example into early DONE or a sharp wrong policy. Or the head's fixed top-left offsets may not match how anchors actually work in this world. This round tests three things: a bigger network with a 3x3 action head and the mask as an input; the same network with stronger exploration; and a global attention trunk.

### Round 4
All 9 trials scored 0 on dev and 0 on training success. None failed or timed out, and each took about 60–70 s. The recipes ranged from 1 to 4 epochs, 131k to 410k steps, gamma 0.95 to 0.99, entropy 0.003 to 0.03 and lr 7e-4 to 2e-3, with no effect. Wider 2D trunks, global broadcast, mask inputs, footprint-concat heads and a transformer also scored 0. So sample count is not the bottleneck, and nothing has shown any measurable learning. These networks probably struggle to work out which layer a brick lands on and then to compare target and build at that layer. They have to do this from a column compressed into one feature vector. Untested idea for this final round: run the same small network once per layer, with weights shared across layers. Each per-layer copy sees that layer's build/target/missing/extra slices and their neighbours, the full column, and a one-hot layer index. Footprint-concat scores are then pooled over layers with logsumexp. Compute stays at r≈1–1.8, using 2D convolutions only.
